questionText: Listen to a conversation between a student and a writing center coordinator.
audioScript:
Situation: A student visits the campus writing center to schedule an appointment for help with a research essay.
Coordinator: Welcome to the Writing Center. How can I help you today?
Kevin: Hi, I'd like to make an appointment to get feedback on my research essay for my history class. It's due in two weeks.
Coordinator: Sure. We offer both in-person and online sessions. Each session is forty-five minutes long. Which format do you prefer?
Kevin: I think in-person would be better. I have a hard copy with my professor's comments that I'd like the tutor to look at.
Coordinator: That works well. Let me check our availability. We have openings this Thursday at two PM and Friday at ten AM. Which one works for you?
Kevin: Friday at ten sounds great. Will the tutor be able to help me with my thesis statement? That's the part I'm struggling with most.
Coordinator: Absolutely. Our tutors are trained to help with thesis development, organization, citations, and grammar. Just bring your assignment prompt and any drafts you have.
Kevin: I'll bring everything. Do I need to prepare anything before the session?
Coordinator: It helps if you read through your draft beforehand and jot down two or three specific questions. That way the tutor can focus on what you need most. Also, please arrive five minutes early to check in at the front desk.
Kevin: Got it. Is there a cancellation policy? Something might come up.
Coordinator: Yes, we ask that you cancel at least twelve hours in advance. If you miss two appointments without cancelling, your account gets suspended for the rest of the semester.
Kevin: That's fair. I'll make sure to cancel ahead of time if anything changes. Thanks for your help!
Coordinator: You're welcome. You'll get a confirmation email shortly. Good luck with your essay.

questionText: Listen to a conversation between a student and a career counselor at career services.
audioScript:
Situation: A junior student visits the Career Services office to get help preparing for a summer internship search.
Counselor: Good morning! I'm Ms. Patterson, one of the career counselors here. What brings you in today?
Jenny: Hi, I'm a junior majoring in marketing, and I want to apply for summer internships. I'm not sure where to start, and my resume feels outdated.
Counselor: That's a great reason to come in. Let's start with your resume. Do you have a copy with you?
Jenny: Yes, I brought a printed copy. I last updated it during my freshman year, so it only has my part-time campus job and a couple of high school activities.
Counselor: Okay. For a marketing internship, you'll want to highlight any relevant coursework, projects, and skills like social media management or data analysis. Have you done any class projects that involved market research or campaign design?
Jenny: Actually, yes. Last semester I did a group project where we created a full marketing campaign for a local coffee shop. We analyzed their target audience and designed social media content.
Counselor: That's excellent experience. You should feature that prominently. I'd also recommend creating a LinkedIn profile if you don't have one yet. Many recruiters search for candidates there.
Jenny: I don't have one yet. Is there a workshop for that?
Counselor: Yes, we're running a LinkedIn and personal branding workshop next Wednesday from three to four-thirty PM in room two-fifty. I can sign you up right now.
Jenny: That would be great. Also, is there a job board where I can find internship listings?
Counselor: Absolutely. Our online portal, CareerConnect, has listings specifically from employers looking to hire our students. You can filter by major, industry, and location. I'll send you the login instructions after this meeting.
Jenny: Perfect. How soon should I start applying?
Counselor: For summer internships, I recommend starting now. Many companies have deadlines in February and March. The earlier you apply, the better your chances.

questionText: Listen to a conversation between a student and a nurse at the student health center.
audioScript:
Situation: A student visits the campus student health center complaining of a persistent sore throat and fever.
Nurse: Good morning. What seems to be the problem today?
Marcus: Hi. I've had a sore throat for about four days now, and since yesterday I've been running a fever. I thought it would go away, but it's getting worse.
Nurse: I'm sorry to hear that. Let me take your temperature first. Okay, it reads one hundred and one point two degrees Fahrenheit. That's a mild fever. Any other symptoms?
Marcus: Yeah, I've had a headache and some body aches. Also, it hurts when I swallow.
Nurse: I see. Have you noticed any white spots on the back of your throat or any swelling in your neck?
Marcus: I'm not sure. I tried looking in the mirror but couldn't really tell. My neck does feel a little swollen on the sides though.
Nurse: Alright. Based on your symptoms, I'd like to do a quick strep test. It takes about ten minutes to get results. If it's positive, the doctor can prescribe antibiotics.
Marcus: Okay. If it's not strep, what could it be?
Nurse: It could be a viral infection, in which case antibiotics won't help. You'd need to rest, drink plenty of fluids, and take over-the-counter pain relievers. We also recommend gargling with warm salt water for the throat pain.
Marcus: I've been taking ibuprofen, but it only helps temporarily. Should I skip classes today?
Nurse: Given your fever, I'd recommend staying home and resting for at least twenty-four hours after the fever breaks. I can write you a note for your professors. Do you have any medication allergies?
Marcus: I'm allergic to penicillin. I get a rash from it.
Nurse: I'll note that in your chart. If the strep test is positive, the doctor will prescribe an alternative antibiotic like azithromycin. Please have a seat in the waiting area and I'll call you in shortly.

questionText: Listen to a conversation between a prospective student and a campus tour guide.
audioScript:
Situation: A prospective student and her father join a campus tour led by a student tour guide on a Saturday morning.
Tour Guide: Welcome, everyone! My name is Brian, and I'll be your tour guide today. I'm a senior studying environmental science. Before we start, does anyone have any questions?
Aisha: Hi Brian. I'm Aisha, and this is my dad. I'm thinking about applying for the environmental science program. Can you tell me what the labs are like?
Tour Guide: Great question, Aisha! Our environmental science labs are held in the Reynolds Science Building, which was renovated just two years ago. We have state-of-the-art equipment for water and soil analysis. Lab sections usually have about fifteen students, so you get a lot of hands-on time.
Aisha: That sounds amazing. What about research opportunities for undergraduates?
Tour Guide: There are plenty. Professor Liu runs an undergraduate research program every summer where students do fieldwork at the nearby lake. You can earn three credits and a small stipend. I participated last summer and it was a fantastic experience.
Aisha's Dad: How competitive is admission to the program?
Tour Guide: The overall university acceptance rate is about forty-five percent. For the environmental science major specifically, it's a bit more selective at around thirty percent. Strong grades in biology and chemistry help a lot.
Aisha: What about housing? Do freshmen have to live on campus?
Tour Guide: Yes, all freshmen are required to live on campus. There are four freshman dormitories, and you can request a roommate or be matched with one. Most rooms are doubles, meaning two students per room.
Aisha: Is there a meal plan requirement for freshmen?
Tour Guide: Yes, freshmen must have at least the fourteen-meal-per-week plan. You can upgrade to unlimited if you prefer. The main dining hall is right next to the freshman dorms, which is very convenient.
Aisha: That's really helpful. Thank you, Brian!
Tour Guide: You're welcome! Let's start walking toward the science building so you can see the labs firsthand.

questionText: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian about booking a study room.
audioScript:
Situation: A student approaches the library front desk to book a group study room for a project meeting.
Priya: Excuse me, I'd like to book a group study room for this evening. Is that possible?
Librarian: Of course. Study rooms can be booked by any currently enrolled student. How many people will be in your group?
Priya: There will be five of us. We're working on a group presentation for our economics class.
Librarian: In that case, you'll need one of our large rooms. We have rooms that seat six to eight people. The small rooms only seat four, so they won't work for your group.
Priya: A large room sounds perfect. What times are available this evening?
Librarian: Let me check the system. For tonight, we have room two-twelve available from six to eight PM, and room three-oh-five available from seven to nine PM. Which would you prefer?
Priya: I think six to eight works better. Can we book room two-twelve?
Librarian: Sure. I'll need your student ID to process the booking. The maximum booking length is two hours per group per day. Is this a one-time booking or will you need it regularly?
Priya: We'll probably need it every Tuesday and Thursday for the next three weeks. Can we make recurring reservations?
Librarian: Yes, recurring reservations are allowed up to four weeks in advance. I can set that up for you now. Just keep in mind that if your group doesn't show up within fifteen minutes of your start time, the reservation is automatically cancelled.
Priya: That's good to know. What happens if we need to cancel a session?
Librarian: You can cancel through the online booking portal or by calling us. There's no penalty for cancelling, but please do it at least two hours ahead so other groups can use the room.
Priya: Understood. Can we eat in the study rooms?
Librarian: Covered drinks are allowed, but no food. If you need to eat, there's a cafe on the first floor. Also, please make sure to leave the room clean and push in the chairs when you're done.
Priya: Will do. Thank you for all the information.

questionText: Listen to a conversation between a student and a dining hall manager about a complaint.
audioScript:
Situation: A student visits the dining services office to file a complaint about food quality and cleanliness issues at the main dining hall.
Dining Manager: Hello, I'm Mr. Thompson, the dining hall manager. How can I help you today?
Sofia: Hi, Mr. Thompson. I'm Sofia. I eat at the main dining hall almost every day, and over the past two weeks I've noticed the quality of the hot meals has really gone downhill. The vegetables are often overcooked and cold, and last Tuesday the chicken seemed undercooked.
Dining Manager: I'm very sorry to hear that. That's certainly not the standard we aim for. Can you tell me what time you usually visit the dining hall?
Sofia: I usually come around seven PM for dinner. I know it's close to closing time, but the food should still be fresh.
Dining Manager: You're absolutely right. Our dinner service runs until eight-thirty, so food at seven should still be at proper temperature. I'll speak with the kitchen staff about monitoring food temperatures more closely, especially during the last hour of service. Was there anything else?
Sofia: Yes, actually. Last Wednesday I noticed several tables hadn't been wiped down, and there was food left on the floor near the salad bar. It seemed like there weren't enough staff cleaning up.
Dining Manager: I appreciate you bringing this to my attention. We've had two student workers call in sick this week, which has put a strain on our cleaning schedule. I'm hiring three new student workers starting next Monday, which should help. In the meantime, I'll assign an additional staff member to monitor the dining area during peak hours.
Sofia: I understand staffing can be difficult. I also wanted to ask if it's possible to get more vegetarian hot options. Right now there's usually only one vegetarian entree, and it's often just pasta.
Dining Manager: That's a fair point. I'll bring it up with our nutrition committee at their next meeting on Friday. We've been planning to add a rotating vegetarian station with different cuisines. I'll make sure it gets prioritized.
Sofia: Thank you for taking my concerns seriously. I really appreciate it.
Dining Manager: Of course. I'll also send you a follow-up email next week to let you know what changes we've implemented. Your feedback helps us improve.

questionText: Listen to a conversation between a student and a box office attendant about campus event tickets.
audioScript:
Situation: A student visits the campus box office to purchase tickets for the upcoming spring concert and asks about discount policies.
Box Office Attendant: Welcome to the campus box office. How can I help you today?
Tyler: Hi, I'd like to buy tickets for the spring concert next Saturday. I heard there's a student discount.
Box Office Attendant: Yes, there is. The spring concert features a local jazz band and a guest vocalist. General admission is twenty-five dollars, but students with a valid ID get a forty percent discount, bringing the price to fifteen dollars per ticket. How many tickets would you like?
Tyler: I'd like three tickets. Two for me and my roommate, and one for my sister who's visiting from out of town. She's not a student here, though.
Box Office Attendant: That's fine. The student discount applies to anyone with a valid student ID from any accredited institution. Does your sister have a student ID from her own university?
Tyler: Actually, yes, she does. She goes to State College. Would that work?
Box Office Attendant: It would, but she'll need to present her ID at the door on the night of the concert. For now, I can sell you all three at the student rate, but I'll note that one ID is pending verification.
Tyler: Perfect. Are there assigned seats or is it general admission?
Box Office Attendant: The main floor is general admission, meaning first-come, first-served seating. The balcony has assigned seats, but those are thirty dollars at the student rate and they're almost sold out. Only balcony seats in rows S through V are still available.
Tyler: Hmm, the balcony seats might be too far back. We'll go with general admission on the main floor. Can we pick up the tickets at will-call on the day of the concert?
Box Office Attendant: Absolutely. I can also print them now or email them to you as mobile tickets. Which do you prefer?
Tyler: Mobile tickets would be great. You can send them to my student email.
Box Office Attendant: Done. I'll send all three tickets to your email. The doors open at six-thirty PM, and the concert starts at seven-thirty. I'd recommend arriving by six to get good seats on the main floor.
Tyler: Got it. Is there a refund policy in case we can't make it?
Box Office Attendant: Refunds are available up to forty-eight hours before the event. After that, you can exchange your tickets for another campus event of equal value, but no cash refunds. Would you like me to note that on your receipt?
Tyler: Yes, please. And I'll pay with my student account.

questionText: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the ID card office.
audioScript:
Situation: A student visits the campus ID card office to replace a malfunctioning student ID card that no longer scans properly.
Staff Member: Good afternoon. Welcome to the ID Card Office. What can I do for you?
Grace: Hi, my student ID card stopped working. The magnetic strip seems damaged because it won't scan at the dining hall or the library anymore. I've been having issues for about a week.
Staff Member: I see. Let me take a look at it. Yes, the magnetic strip is significantly worn down. This happens over time with regular use. When did you first get this card?
Grace: I got it at the beginning of my freshman year, so about two and a half years ago. I use it every day for meals, building access, and printing, so it gets a lot of wear.
Staff Member: That explains it. We generally recommend replacing cards every two years if you use them heavily. Since this is normal wear and tear, not loss or intentional damage, there's no replacement fee.
Grace: Oh, that's a relief. I was worried I'd have to pay. My friend had to pay fifteen dollars when she lost hers.
Staff Member: That's correct. Lost or stolen cards have a fifteen-dollar fee, but malfunctioning cards from normal use are replaced free of charge. Now, I'll need to take a new photo for your replacement card. The system doesn't reuse old photos.
Grace: Sure. Should I remove my glasses?
